## Stage Overview

In this lab, participants develop an initial research workflow using brain and behavioral data. Using AI-assisted development tools, you will build a four-stage automated workflow that imports research data, performs signal analysis, generates a visualization dashboard, and creates a reproducibility documentation file. No prior programming experience is required — you will act as a **Workflow Designer**, using structured AI prompting to build and refine each stage.

## How Data Flows Through the Workflow

The four stages of a reproducible research workflow are connected as follows:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
graph LR
    A("1. Obtaining Data") -->|Data Stream| B("2. Analyzing Data")
    B -->|Decoded Trajectories| C("3. Visualizing Results")
    C -->|Tracking Accuracy| D("4. Documenting Research")
```

***

## The Four Stages of This Lab

### Stage 1 — Obtaining Data
Connect to an open brain and behavioral research dataset, load the recordings into the workflow, and verify that the data is complete and ready for analysis. This stage does not perform any calculations — it only prepares the data.

### Stage 2 — Analyzing Data
Apply a signal decoding method to extract movement trajectory information from the neural signal recordings. The analysis runs entirely within this stage and passes its results forward — it does not load data or create any plots.

### Stage 3 — Visualizing Results
Build a live accuracy tracking dashboard that shows how well the decoded trajectories match the expected movement targets. The dashboard updates as the analysis runs.

### Stage 4 — Documenting Research
Automatically generate a structured documentation file that records the analysis settings used, the accuracy results obtained, and the software environment — creating a reproducible record of exactly what was done.

***

## Laboratory Playground

The **Laboratory Playground** at the end of this lab gives you a safe space to explore how changes in analysis settings affect your results. Try adjusting the signal processing parameters and observe how the accuracy dashboard and documentation file respond. This is where the most important learning happens — not just running a workflow, but understanding *why* it behaves the way it does.
